paper_title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Sable: Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models Tomer Solberg MoonMath.ai research@moonmath.ai Abstract We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that committed, integer-quantized transformer produced given token sequence from given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function FO without any floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. Within one domain, the proof batches zerochecks and the leaf layer of LogUp-GKR lookups into single sumcheck. Lookups are split into chunks of fewer than lookups, which LogUp needs for soundness in prime field. Every witness tensor and weight lives in one multilinear commitment, built from rate-1/2 ReedSolomon code, BLAKE3 Merkle trees of mixed height, and mixed-length BaseFold opening over the degree-8 extension. The prover streams the model layer by layer in two passes, recomputes the witness where it would otherwise store it, and runs on one GPU with device-resident FiatShamir transcript and CUDA-graph replay of identical layers. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 for one sequence of 4,096 tokens, 253 for four such sequences, and 398 for one sequence of 16,384 tokens. The same prover covers Qwen3-32B, which adds QK-norm, and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B, proving 4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s. proof takes 41 to 50 times as long as computing the same tokens in our serving engine for FO, or 6.4 cents for 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. The price of exactness is accuracy: on WikiText-2, FOs greedy token matches the BF16 models at 86.3% of positions and its perplexity is 8.3% higher; we trace about third of this gap to the 8-bit queries and keys. On Qwen3, choosing per key-value group how the score exponent is split between queries and keys, which costs nothing in the proof, removes 53% of the perplexity gap of Qwen3-30B-A3B and 23% of that of Qwen3-32B, and on both models FO is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. We reduce the work of the verifier, which recursive compression must arithmetize, from 17.8 to 4.2 million BLAKE3 compressions for 4,096-token proof of the full model, and verifier with compiled core checks the proofs of all three models on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. We also give BLAKE3 circuit in the same proof system, whose constraint proof costs 2.8 µs per compression. In the random-oracle model and with proven proximity bounds, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2103, counting 30-bit proof of work on the queries. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system as built is meant for open-weight models and for verifiers, such as auditors, that can afford proof of 106 to 477 MiB. The prover, the verifier and the scripts behind every measurement are available under the MIT license at https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A client that sends prompt to hosted language model receives text and nothing else. It cannot tell which model produced the text, whether the weights were quantized more aggressively than advertised, whether the answer was cut short, or whether the sampling decisions were made with the randomness it was promised. Verifiable inference asks the server to attach evidence that the output equals (W, x, r) for the prompt x, sampling seed the server did not choose, and weights fixed by public commitment CW . The evidence can come from trusted hardware, from re-execution by other parties, from statistical fingerprints of the computation, or from cryptographic proof. Only the last gives guarantee that rests on cryptographic assumptions alone and can be checked by anyone, at any later time, without the weights. Cryptographic proofs of neural network inference have so far been costly. Systems based on sumcheck and GKR proved convolutional networks [LXZ21] and later language models with up to 13 billion parameters in under fifteen minutes per inference [SLZ24]. Circuit-based systems compile models into general-purpose SNARKs [CWSK24, Zko23]. Three obstacles separate these results from proving the inference that server actually performs on production-size model. The function must be exact. proof establishes relation between integers or field elements. Floating-point inference is not function of its inputs in that sense: results change with the kernel, the batch shape and the order of reductions [HT25], and single changed argmax or sampling decision changes every later token. proof system therefore needs precisely defined integer function , and the server must serve that function. Approximate checks of the floating-point computation, as in [OFP+25], answer different question. The constraints must not wrap. Small prime fields make provers fast, since base-field element fits machine word and arithmetic needs no multi-precision code [Pol24, HLP24, BDT24]. They also make every intermediate quantity of transformer large compared to p: dot product of 215 products of 8-bit integers reaches 229, and softmax denominator over 220 keys reaches 230, against 231. relation that holds modulo but not over the integers lets prover change the computation and still pass. Every relation must therefore be accompanied by bounds that keep both sides below p. The proof must scale. For one 16,384-token sequence through Qwen2.5-32B, the trace has about 6 1011 committed field elements and 7 1011 lookups. This trace does not fit in GPU memory or in host memory, and the number of lookups exceeds p, so the multiset argument of LogUp [Hab22] is unsound unless the lookups are partitioned.

sections.title: 1.1 Contributions
sections.content: An exact integer transformer (Section 5). We define FO, an integer function for Qwen2style decoder-only transformers, and extend it to the QK-norm and mixture-of-experts layers of Qwen3. Activations are 24-bit, matrix products take 8-bit inputs with power-of-two scales placed off the reduction axis, and attention and the MLP use fused rounding steps. Sampling, greedy or by inverse CDF, reads seed derived from client nonce. deterministic program maps BF16 checkpoint to FO. wrap-free constraint system over 31-bit field (Section 6). Every gadget comes with integer bounds, under which the relation over Fp is equivalent to the relation over 4 (Theorem 6.1). Every gadget also has exactly one satisfying output (Theorem 6.2). Range and table checks go through one tagged table of 226 rows. streamed proof built from three primitives (Section 7). domain proves the zerocheck and the leaf layer of the LogUp-GKR trees of set of columns in one sumcheck (Theorem 7.1). Lookups are split into chunks of at most 230 lookups, each with its own multiplicity column, and one GKR over the table proves all chunks at once (Theorem 7.2). Claims flow backward from the output to the embedding, so the prover makes two passes over the model and never holds more than one layers witness. All tensors and weights live in one multilinear commitment whose openings are batched across sizes and whose Merkle paths are shared across the tensors of layer. single-GPU prover (Section 9). Sumcheck round kernels are generated per constraint program and run their first rounds on base-field tables. The FiatShamir transcript runs on the GPU, one warp per BLAKE3 compression, so the prove pass has no host round trips. One middle layers prove pass is captured as CUDA graph and replayed for the other layers. Fp4 products use one modular reduction per coordinate. verifier that recursion can afford (Section 10). Public columns are evaluated in closed form, fixed tables are committed, final openings are recorded without being hashed into the transcript, and tensors share columns and Merkle paths. Together these steps cut the verifiers hashing by 4.2, and the proof for 4,096 tokens from 360 to 134.8 MiB. We also build the first component of the recursive circuit: BLAKE3 compressions as rows of domain, with LogUp memory that wires the rows together. Evaluation and analysis (Sections 8 and 11). We measure the prover on all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B and on Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, relate its time to the inference it attests and to prior systems, measure what exactness costs in accuracy and which integer steps cause the loss, and give soundness analysis with every term of the error budget. The analysis of tuple compression in LogUp (Theorem 8.1) shows that compressing tuple of arity with the powers of one challenge costs log 2 bits, so Sable draws one challenge per tuple coordinate. The implementation, its tests and the scripts that produce every measurement in this paper are released under the MIT license at https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable.

sections.title: 1.2 Scope
sections.content: The main proof is not zero-knowledge: it reveals evaluations of the trace to its verifier. It is large, 134.8 MiB for one 4,096-token sequence through the full model, and verifier with compiled core takes 19 on one CPU core to check it. As built, Sable therefore produces an auditors proof for open-weight models: non-zero-knowledge proof that reopens the committed weights would leak closed weights after about 2 104 proofs. Section 4 states the threat model, the trust anchors of the verifier and these limits. recursive layer that proves the verifier, with zero-knowledge outer layers, is the intended form for every client; Section 10 reports the parts of it that exist. The statement concerns FO itself, and the BF16 checkpoint it was derived from plays no role in it, so the accuracy of FO relative to the original model is part of what deployment must report (Section 11.8).

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Proofs of machine-learning inference. Early systems proved small networks with generalpurpose SNARKs or with interactive proofs specialized to matrix products. zkCNN [LXZ21] introduced sumcheck-based argument for convolutions, building on the GKR line of work. Mystique [WYX+21] used VOLE-based interactive zero-knowledge proofs with conversions between arithmetic and Boolean values. ZKML [CWSK24] and ezkl [Zko23] compile models to Halo2 circuits and optimize the circuit layout. For language models, zkLLM [SLZ24] combines sumcheck for tensor operations with lookup argument (tlookup) for non-arithmetic operations and dedicated protocol for attention; it proves models up to 13B parameters and outputs short proofs through pairing-based commitment. zkGPT [QSL+25] targets GPT-2-sized models with optimized constraint layouts for non-linear functions and proves GPT-2 in about 22 on CPU. Section 11.4 compares proving times per parameter and token. zkLLM and zkGPT work over large prime fields (BLS12-381 or BN254 scalar fields), where single field element holds any intermediate value, and both approximate non-linear functions without fixing the integer semantics of the served model. Sable differs in three respects: it works over 31-bit field and pays for that with explicit no-wrap bounds; it defines the served function bit for bit, including normalization, softmax, sampling and stopping; and it targets models and contexts large enough that the trace must be streamed. Concurrent work. FlashProve [Ant26, RAC+26], concurrent system from Anthropic, proves inference of Llama 4 Maverick, mixture of experts with 400.7B parameters of which token uses 16.15B, from third-party 4-bit release of its weights. It replaces the model by an integer function with table-based non-linear steps, as we do, and compiles interactive oracle proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field with ReedSolomon codes, BLAKE2b Merkle trees and zero-knowledge proximity tests; the proof hides the weights, it is about 18.8 MB per request, and the soundness, completeness and zero knowledge of the protocol are proved in Lean, while its C++ and CUDA programs are tested. On one H100 it proves 1,024-token windows at about 111 tokens per second in batches of 24; under its default policy proof checks one token, the greedy successor of the window, and an optional policy checks every token of stored reply against looser criterion than greedy choice. Sable differs in what it proves and where it is measured. Sable proof covers whole reply: every generated token, the stopping rule, and, at positive temperature, sampling from seed fixed by the statement, FlashProve does not check sampling, and reply cut short verifies there as shorter reply. Sable proves contexts of up to 16,384 tokens, where attention, quadratic in the length, is about half of the work, against 1,024 there. Our commitment to the weights is plain Merkle root that anyone can recompute from an open checkpoint and that serves any number of proofs, while FlashProves hiding commitment bounds the number of batches it can serve, at most 688,127. We report the accuracy of the integer model on full task benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K) against BF16 and two deployed 8-bit schemes; FlashProve reports how often its greedy token differs from the 16-bit models on WikiText-2 (6.8% and 9.4% of positions on two text sets) and runs no task benchmark. Its prover needs about 260 GB of host memory, against at most 188 GB (175 GiB) for ours. Per active parameter and token, FlashProves mixture of experts takes about as long as Sables dense proofs and 6 to 11 times less than Sables proofs of Qwen3-30B-A3B (Section 11.4), with zero knowledge included and at shorter context. FlashProves zero knowledge, proofs 6 to 27 times smaller than ours, faster proofs of mixture of experts with about twelve times as many parameters as our models, and machine-checked protocol mark directions of future work for Sable: zero-knowledge and recursive layers that shrink the proof (Sections 10 and 12), proofs of larger mixtures of experts at lower cost per active parameter, and machine-checked proof of the protocol. 6 Other approaches to trustworthy inference. Trusted execution environments on GPUs attest to the code that ran, under hardware trust assumption. Refereed delegation [CRR11] and optimistic schemes resolve disputes by re-execution, which requires deterministic computation and an honest party with the weights. TOPLOC [OFP+25] hashes features of the floating-point activations so that verifier with the model can check, approximately and statistically, that claimed computation was performed. Our statement is exact and our verifier does not need the weights, at much higher proving cost. Sumcheck, GKR and lookups. The sumcheck protocol [LFKN92] and the GKR protocol [GKR15] underlie provers whose cost is linear in the computation. Thaler [Tha13] gave linear-time provers for matrix products and regular circuits; Libra [XZZ+19] made GKR linear-time for general circuits and added zero knowledge; Spartan [Set20] and HyperPlonk [CBBZ23] built SNARKs for constraint systems around zerochecks over the Boolean hypercube. Lookup arguments started with Plookup [GW20]; LogUp [Hab22] replaced grand products by sums of logarithmic derivatives, and Papini and Haböck [PH23] proved those sums with GKR, which removes any commitment that depends on the lookup challenge. Lasso and Jolt [STW24, AST24] use structured tables and sumcheck-based lookups for virtual machines. Our domains combine the last GKR layer of all lookups with the zerocheck of the same columns in one sumcheck, and our chunking follows from the observation that LogUp only proves inclusion modulo the characteristic. Small fields and sumcheck prover algorithms. STARK provers moved from 64-bit fields to 31-bit fields (Mersenne-31, BabyBear, KoalaBear) for speed on CPUs and GPUs [Pol24, HLP24]; Binius [DP25] works over binary towers. In all of them, soundness needs challenges from an extension field. Gruen [Gru24] showed how to remove the equality factor from zerocheck round messages and how to skip the first rounds extension arithmetic. Bagad, Domb and Thaler [BDT24] and Dao et al. [DDB+26] gave sumcheck provers that keep most work in the base field when the summed polynomials take small values. Our prover evaluates the first round of every sumcheck on base-field tables and folds them into extension tables in the second round; the more aggressive small-value algorithms of [BDT24, DDB+26] would apply to our constraint programs only with extension-field coefficients, which Section 9.2 discusses. Hash-based polynomial commitments. FRI [BSBHR18a] tests proximity to ReedSolomon codes and underlies STARKs [BSBHR18b]; its soundness up to the Johnson bound follows from the proximity gaps of Ben-Sasson et al. [BSCI+20], and Haböck [Hab24] analyzes BaseFold over ReedSolomon codes in the same list-decoding regime. Multilinear commitments from linear codes include Ligero [AHIV17] and Brakedown [GLS+23]; BaseFold [ZCF24] folds foldable code alongside sumcheck, and WHIR [ACFY25] reduces the verifiers queries. Our commitment uses BaseFold over ReedSolomon codes on multiplicative subgroups, batches columns of different lengths by joining them at the matching fold level, as in batched FRI for mixed degrees, and arranges all columns of layer under one Merkle tree whose height differs per column size. GPU provers. GPU acceleration of proof systems has concentrated on multi-scalar multiplication and number-theoretic transforms for pairing-based SNARKs [MXS+23, LWY+23] and on STARK provers over small fields (for example sppark and ICICLE). Sables kernels are generated per constraint program and per field, and its transcript runs on the GPU, so that the whole prove pass of layer can be replayed as one CUDA graph. 7 Integer-only inference fixes the arithmetic of network so Integer inference and quantization. that it runs on integer units [JKC+18, KGY+21]. LLM.int8() [DLBZ22], SmoothQuant [XLS+23], QuaRot [AMC+24] and SpinQuant [LZF+25] quantize transformers to 8 bits or fewer by handling activation outliers, through mixed precision, scale migration or rotations. FO uses random orthogonal rotation fused into the weights in the manner of QuaRot, per-row dynamic exponents for activations, and per-column exponents for weights, and it replaces every floating-point non-linearity with table. Incrementally verifiable computation [Val08] and recursive SNARKs compress long Recursion. proofs by proving their verifier. Hash-based recursion that evaluates the hash inside the circuit is standard for STARKs and is usually paired with an algebraic hash; we keep BLAKE3 everywhere, which makes the recursion circuit larger and avoids further hash assumption.

sections.title: 4 Threat Model and Scope
sections.content: Adversary and trust anchors. The adversary is the server, which runs the prover and wants verifier to accept an output that is not FO(W, x, r) for the committed . The verifier trusts three things. (i) registry that publishes, with the model release, CW and digest hcirc of every constant outside the weights (exponents, shifts, biases, tables and the commitment digests of the fixed tables). For an open-weight model anyone recomputes both from the checkpoint and the published quantization program, so the registry needs no trust beyond that recomputation. The server must never be the source of either, since server that supplies hcirc chooses the tables. (ii) Its own tokenization: the statement is over token ids, so the client tokenizes and must receive the full sequence, including any system prompt the server prepends; proof over sequence with hidden prefix proves different statement and is rejected. (iii) Its nonce nc, which fixes the sampling seed. Who verifies. The proof is not zero-knowledge, it is 106 to 477 MiB long for the three models we evaluate, and our verifier takes 19 to 56 on one CPU core (Section 11.7). As built, it is therefore an auditors proof: the verifier is client or an auditor that can afford this, for model whose weights are public. recursive proof of the verifier with zero-knowledge outer layers is the intended form for every client, and Section 10 reports its first components. Open weights. The proof reveals the trace at the queried positions, and the weights are committed once and reopened by every proof. The cheap checks come first: the statement and policy checks before the transcript starts, and the caps of the weight and fixed units against CW and the fixed digests before any sumcheck, so proof for other weights or tables fails before any expensive work. It checks every sumcheck and GKR round, the per-chunk and per-set fraction sums, the claims on public columns (index columns, causal masks, one-hot and prefix indicators of the targets, all in closed form with O(log) work), the caps of the weight and fixed units against CW and the fixed digests, the unit openings, the global sumcheck, the folds, both proof-of-work nonces, and every query. sections.title: 8.3 Soundness
sections.content: Theorem 8.4 (Soundness). Model BLAKE3 as random oracle. Let st be statement whose CW commits to valid model (weights in [127, 127] and embedding rows in A, as produced by the program of Section 5.7), and such that no committed by CW satisfies (st, ) R. Then any prover that makes at most random-oracle queries makes the Sable verifier accept st with probability at most ϵrbr + O(Q2/2256), where ϵrbr 2103.4 is the maximum of the terms in Table 2. Here query counts once per evaluation of the transcript hash, and the proofs of work make each attempt at the two challenges they precede cost 230 and 211 evaluations: without them the two tightest terms are ϵquery = (p1/2 + 0.01)153 = 273.4 and ϵLU = 292.9 per attempt. Proof sketch. We show that the underlying IOP has round-by-round soundness error ϵrbr; the theorem then follows from the analysis of the FiatShamir transform for such IOPs [CCH+19, BSCS16], with the O(Q2/2256) term accounting for hash collisions in the Merkle trees (Theorem 8.2). The state function of the round-by-round analysis is the following predicate. Call partial transcript doomed if some claim it contains is false with respect to the committed oracles: claim on columns multilinear extension, sumcheck or GKR claim, fraction sum, or recorded opening claim. Every term of Table 2 is the probability that one challenge turns doomed transcript into one that is not, so it is per-round escape probability; none of them is union bound over whole proof. 1 4K proof draws about 5.1 105 challenges  (Table 11)  , and ϵrbr bounds the escape probability 30 at each of them. In particular, the LogUp test is single round for all chunks: and the coefficients β are drawn once, after all multiplicities are committed, and doomed transcript escapes only if the identity of chunk that contains bad lookup holds at the drawn point, which Theorem 8.1 bounds for that chunk. By Theorems 6.1 and 6.2, if every constraint, static lookup, gather and output constraint holds for the committed assignment, then the assignment is the execution of FO on the committed weights, and (st, ) R. Hence, for false statement, the committed assignment violates at least one of them, and the statement checks of Section 7.7 reject any assignment that violates none. The first challenge that tests the violated item then makes the transcript doomed except with probability bounded by one term of the budget: Theorem 7.1 for constraints and leaf fractions, Theorems 7.2 and 8.1 for lookups and gathers, Theorem 3.1 for each product and reduction sumcheck, and the zerocheck bound for the output constraints. Each later round keeps doomed transcript doomed except with probability at most the corresponding per-round term, since false claim entering sumcheck round yields false claim leaving it unless the verifiers challenge hits root of nonzero polynomial of the stated degree. At the end, doomed transcript contains false claim on committed column, which the global evaluation proof rejects except with the probability of Theorem 8.3. Weight binding. CW is the digest of the weight units caps, so by Theorem 8.2 proof that verifies against CW is bound to one committed weight assignment. The proof does not check the ranges of the committed weights; they are property of CW , established by whoever computes it. For open weights, anyone recomputes CW from the published checkpoint and quantization program, which also establishes the ranges. For closed weights the party that computes CW is the one the verifier distrusts, and with out-of-range weights Theorems 6.1 and 6.2 no longer hold; one-time range proof of the committed weights per model release (one lookup per weight, about 3.3 1010 lookups, small fraction of one 16K proofs 7.2 1011) would remove the assumption, and we have not built it. What is not claimed. The main proof is not zero-knowledge: the opened columns and claimed evaluations reveal information about the trace and about the weights. The weight codewords are fixed and every proof opens them at fresh positions, so about 1.9 104 proofs reveal enough codeword symbols to recover every weight column by linear algebra (Section 4); the system as built is for open-weight models. The statement concerns FO: sequence produced by other kernels will in general not satisfy R, because one changed rounding decision changes every later token. Tokens injected by the server after the prompt (tool outputs, retrieved documents) are part of only if the client can check their provenance.

sections.title: 9 A single-GPU prover
sections.content: The prover is written in Python on top of PyTorch, with CUDA kernels compiled at run time by NVRTC. Python orchestrates the protocol, and all arithmetic on witness-sized data runs on the GPU. This section describes the techniques that matter for its speed; Section 11.6 measures them.

sections.title: 9.1 Memory: streaming and recomputation
sections.content: The witness of 16,384-token proof is several terabytes, so no pass keeps it. The commit pass stores only the residual stream at layer boundaries (S values of 32 and 8 bits per layer, in pinned host memory). Each later phase that needs layers witness (the prove pass and the query phase) 31 recomputes it from the stored boundary with the same integer kernels as the forward pass, about 42 ms per layer at 4,096 tokens. The per-layer reduction of Section 7.5 exists to keep this count at three builds per layer (commit, prove, query): without it, the global evaluation proof needed two more full passes over every layer, about 25% of the proving time at every shape. Codewords are never stored either: the commit pass hashes them as it encodes, and the global evaluation proof re-encodes the combined columns. Peak GPU memory is 37 GiB for one 4,096-token sequence and 72 GiB for one 16,384-token sequence. Peak host memory is 100 and 174 GiB; the models 8-bit weights, kept in host memory and streamed to the GPU layer by layer, take about 33 GiB of it, and the boundaries and the pinned pool of the per-layer reduction most of the rest.

sections.title: 9.2 Generated sumcheck kernels
sections.content: Every domain defines polynomial program, the bracket of (1), over its half-columns. The prover turns each program into CUDA kernel that computes one round of the sumcheck. Each thread handles pairs of rows, evaluates the program at the rounds interpolation points {0, 2, . . . , d}, and reduces the results across the grid. Coefficients that depend on challenges are kernel arguments read from shared memory, and format constants that differ per layer come from device buffer, so one compiled kernel serves every layer of model. Large programs (the MLP domain has dozens of columns and degree 10) use 224 to 255 registers per thread, and their rounds are limited by instruction latency while memory bandwidth stays far from saturated. Moving the extension-field coefficients from registers to shared memory reduced spilling and cut the GPU time of layer by 3.6%. Base-field first rounds. All committed values are base-field integers. The first round of every sumcheck reads base-field tables and evaluates the program with base-field arithmetic where its coefficients allow; the second round reads the base table again and folds it twice, with the first two challenges, before writing the quarter-size extension table that the third round reads. The more aggressive small-value algorithms of [BDT24, DDB+26] expand rounds 2 and 3 over Lagrange nodes and need the programs coefficients in the base field. Ours are extension elements (challenge-weighted combinations of constraints and lookups), so those algorithms would roughly double the evaluations per pair; our estimate of their gain on top of the current scheme is about 1% of the proof. Lookup leaves. lookup with numerator one contributes a(q0 + q1) + aλq0q1 to (1). We evaluate it as aλ(q0 + µ)(q1 + µ) aµ with µ = 1/λ, folding aλ into the coefficients of q0. This halves the extension multiplications per lookup in the compute-bound first round. GKR rounds. Large GKR rounds run at 83 to 88% of the GPUs memory bandwidth and are close to the roofline for reading, folding and writing the layer. Small rounds (at most 215 pairs) are latency-bound; we spread their (pair, lookup) work items over all blocks of the grid instead of looping over lookups in one thread, which cut the GPU time of layer from 1.01 to 0.90 at 4,096 tokens.

sections.title:
9.3 Field arithmetic
Base-field products use Barrett reduction of 62-bit products. For Fp4 = Fp[Y ]/(Y 4 − 3) we use the
schoolbook product with the factor 3 folded into one operand: each output coordinate is a sum of
four products below p2, so the sum is below 4p2 < 264 and needs a single reduction. This raised
the measured throughput of Fp4 multiplications from 255 to 371 billion per second on our GPU
sections.content: 32 (one reduction per coordinate against Karatsuba over Fp2 with six reductions), and cut the MLP domains sumcheck from 40.8 to 36.6 ms. An instruction count had predicted no gain, because the 64-bit Barrett reduction costs more than the multiplications it saves. Fp8 uses Karatsuba over the faster Fp4; delayed reduction does not fit in 64 bits there, since eight products would be summed per coordinate. The same delayed reduction in the linear-combination kernel of the commitment brings it to the memory bandwidth limit (4.79 3.83 ms for 128 columns of 223). α Opening kernels. unit opening needs, for every column, its value at the reduced point ρ, and the combination kfk folded at the high coordinates of ρ. Computing the values as dot products with full eq(ρ, ) table reads 16 bytes of table per 4-byte column element. One kernel instead folds every column at the high coordinates with table of at most 212 entries, reading each column once; the values and the folded combination follow from the folded vectors of at most 211 entries. This cut the proving time of 8 layers by 1.6% at 4,096 tokens and 2.4% at 16,384 tokens.

sections.title: 9.4 A device-resident transcript
sections.content: A sumcheck round needs the transcript between two kernels: absorb the round message, squeeze the challenge, fold. With the transcript on the host, each round costs device-to-host copy and synchronization, and the prove pass of one layer at 4,096 tokens has several thousand rounds. Sable keeps the transcript state (Section 3.5) on the GPU. The last block of each round kernel absorbs the round message and derives the challenge. One warp performs each compression, with lane < 16 holding word of the block, so that block is filled in one step and the compression reads its message through warp shuffles. This brought rounds transcript step from 25.9 to 8.8 µs. The device transcript absorbs exactly the bytes the host transcript would and samples challenges by the same rejection loop, so proofs are byte-identical either way, which the tests check; the verifier always uses the host implementation. The prover never needs the values of the claims it produces, since they matter only to the verifiers checks. In the prove pass, claimed values, points and coefficients therefore stay on the device as lazy values, and the commitments openings run on the same device transcript. whole layers prove pass then runs without host synchronization.

sections.title: 9.5 Graph replay
sections.content: The prove passes of the middle layers launch the same kernels with the same shapes; only the data differs. Sable captures the prove pass of layer 2 once as CUDA graph and replays it for layers 3, . . . , 1. Before each replay, the inputs are written into fixed buffers: the layers weights, its stored boundary, its format constants, and the incoming claims. After each replay, the outputs are relabeled: claims on layer 1 with shifted challenge indices, the opening states, and the transcript messages. Three rules keep the replay identical to plain run. Every constant that depends on the layer index is read from device buffer. The transcript absorbs the layer index once at the start of the layer, and every later label omits it. Claims that layer makes on the fixed units are replayed per layer from template. The proof is byte-identical to that of the plain prover. At 4,096 tokens, replay brings 64-layer proof from 133 to 106 s, 0.43 per replayed layer; at 16,384 tokens the prover is GPU-bound and the gain is 1%. The gain is larger than the 0.27 of host-side Python time per layer that we measured on 8-layer proofs without replay; we did not isolate the remainder, which may come from the order of kernels in the captured graph.

sections.title: 9.6 Other kernels
sections.content: ReedSolomon encoding uses radix-2 NTT in two passes for codewords up to 224 symbols: the last pass covers up to 13 contiguous bits, the others up to 10, in tiles of 8,192 symbols. Encoding 26 codewords of 224 symbols takes 6.2 ms. Softmax multiplicities come from histogram that the attention witness kernel accumulates in shared memory, which avoids rebuilding the tile domains columns and saved 3% at 16,384 tokens. Multiplicity columns stay on the host as bytes with sparse list of larger entries, and are compressed on side stream.

sections.title: 10 Toward recursive compression
sections.content: A proof of 134.8 MiB is acceptable for an auditor who verifies it once, but too large to return with every response or to publish. The intended form for every client is recursive proof: proof, in the same proof system, that the Sable verifier accepts the main proof. Its outer layers would be zero-knowledge, and the final layer would use low-rate code for short proof. Its cost is set by what the main verifier computes, so this section first reduces the verifiers work and then gives the first circuit component, BLAKE3.

sections.title: 10.1 What the verifier computes
sections.content: We count the verifiers operations by instrumenting the reference verifier. For the full 64-layer model on one 4,096-token sequence, the verifier originally performed 17.8 million BLAKE3 compressions: 10.6 million in the transcript and 7.2 million for Merkle leaves and paths. It also performed about 11 million Fp4 multiplications and, through the public columns it evaluated by folding, about 4.7 109 folded elements per proof. recursive circuit that pays about 4096 trace cells per compression and 16 per extension operation would cost more than third of the main proof. We removed this work in the following steps, each protocol change with its own tests. 1. Closed-form public columns. Every structured public column has an O(log n) closed-form multilinear extension: index columns and (i s) are 2jxj over the kept bits, the causal tile mask [c r] is comparator evaluated from the top bit, and the vocabulary indicators [v < yt], [v = yt] and one-hots are comparators against the constant yt, weighted by eq over the rows. 2. Committed fixed tables. The 226-row table and the RoPE tables are committed once per model and shape as fixed units. The prover sends the tables evaluations, which become claims on these units, and the verifier compares their caps with precomputed digests. On small test model this cut the verifiers folded elements from 4.7 109 to 3 104. 3. Recorded final openings. After the query positions are drawn, nothing else is drawn, so absorbing the leaf values and paths into the transcript binds nothing; they are now recorded in the proof without being hashed. For one layer this reduced the absorbed bytes from 11.0 to 1.5 MiB. 4. Fewer, wider columns. Every query opens every column, so the number of columns, more than the number of committed elements, sets the leaf hashing. Tensors with few small blocks share columns, with padding allowed up to 220 elements; the attention probabilities are packed into wide columns after the prover sends each blocks value at the shared point; the weights are packed flat. Columns fell from 84.8K to 32.6K at cost of 2.5% more committed elements. 34 Configuration Proof BLAKE3 compressions (MiB) Transcript Merkle Total Before the reductions + fixed units, recorded openings, trees per class, small-tensor packing + packing of and the weights + mixed-height trees + per-layer reduction, sequential-mode transcript 360.0 224 154.9 132.5 134.1 10.56M 7.20M 17.77M 4.1M 6.2M 2.1M 2.15M 3.09M 5.24M 2.12M 2.48M 4.60M 1.72M 2.50M 4.22M Table 3: Proof size and verifier BLAKE3 compressions for Qwen2.5-32B, 64 layers, one 4,096-token sequence. The last row is an exact count of the sequential mode (Section 3.5). 5. Shared Merkle paths. layers units share trees, first one per class and then one mixed-height tree per layer (Section 7.5). sections.content: Table 8 normalizes proving time by model size and number of tokens. zkLLM [SLZ24] takes 30.2 ps per parameter and token for LLaMa-2-13B on an A100; Sable takes 0.48 to 0.75 ps on Qwen2.5-32B, 40 to 64 times less. FO is a different function from the BF16 model, and its accuracy determines whether a deployment can
serve it. We compare it with BF16 Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and with two deployed 8-bit quantizations

scales, activations quantized dynamically) and SmoothQuant W8A8 INT8 [XLS+23] (smoothing

activations). FO is evaluated with an engine that computes the same integer function as the
prover’s witness generator, vectorized over heads and sequences, and that we checked to produce

non-overlapping windows of 2,048 tokens covering the whole test split, each evaluated from its first

On MMLU, FO is 1.4 points below BF16 (81.8% against 83.2%; 82.7% against 84.2% averaged over subjects), where FP8 and INT8 lose at most 0.2; on GSM8K, where answers depend on chain of greedy decisions, it is 0.6 points below BF16, against 0.2 and 0.4 for FP8 and INT8. The left-shift regime of Theorem 6.3 is common on real inputs: over the first 16 WikiText-2 windows, 4.1% of the rows of the attention output and down projections have shift 0, and 1.7% true left shift (down to = 8); the logits never do. Honest proofs therefore exercise the input bound of Section 6.2. Where the accuracy goes. To find which of FOs integer steps cost accuracy, we evaluated variants of FO that each make one step more precise and keep the weights, the calibration and every other step  (Table 13)  : float softmax computes the attention probabilities and their normalization in double precision from the same integer scores, instead of as 10-bit values with 16-bit denominator mantissas; 12-bit queries and keys shift by 4 bits less in the ShiftQ8S that produces them and saturate at 16 127, with RoPE and the scores kept at this precision and the softmax scale divided by 28; SiLU with 4 more bits evaluates SiLU in double precision on the same integer input and rounds it with 4 more fractional bits; 16-bit up projection rounds the up projection to 16 bits instead of 8. In the last two, the shift after the gate product grows by the added bits. We also rebuilt FO with the same program calibrated on 8 windows of 1,024 tokens from the WikiText-2 training split, instead of our technical text. Only the queries and keys matter: with 12 bits they remove 37% of the gap to BF16 and raise agreement to 88.6%. The other three changes each move perplexity by less than 3% of the gap, and all four together do no better than the queries and keys alone. Recalibrating on WikiText-2 text changes nothing, so the choice of calibration text does not explain the gap. The remaining 63% lies in steps we did not vary; the 8-bit activations entering every projection and the 8-bit values are the obvious candidates. The variants are not provable as they stand, because the extra bits break bounds of the constraint system. 12-bit queries and keys make scores reach 230, far outside the 223-entry exponential table, so provable version would round each score by shift before the table lookup, adding committed values and lookups to every causal score entry; 16-bit probabilities would make block sum reach 235, above p, and would need each probability committed as two 8-bit limbs. sections.content: The test suite runs every protocol step on small model with the shape of Qwen2 (two layers, width 256, four query and two key-value heads). Besides honest proofs, it checks rejection in five ways. Every message of proof is corrupted in turn, and each corrupted proof must be rejected. proof made with different weights must not verify against CW . proof whose sampled tokens do not follow from the seed must be rejected at temperature θ > 0. Targeted forgeries of the final openings (25 messages and 9 oracle elements) must be rejected. Forgeries of the no-wrap bounds must be rejected: ShiftQ8 row quantized at too-large exponent with wrapped minimality witness, rows whose ShiftQ8S or gate shift exceeds its bound, and left-shift rows built from the residues of Theorem 6.3; so must proof checked against model constants that differ from the provers, and tokens outside the vocabulary. sections.title: 12 Discussion
sections.content: The price of exactness. Sable proves the function server runs, so the server must run FO. FO uses 8-bit matrix products with exact 32-bit accumulation, which integer tensor cores support, but its fused rounding steps, the 9-bit outputs of RoPE8, and the blocked product need their own kernels. We wrote serving engine for it that computes FO bit for bit (checked token by token against the reference implementation): attention is an exact integer kernel in Triton that never forms the score matrix (products of 9-bit integers in fp16 with fp32 accumulation are exact while every partial sum stays below 224, which the blocked product guarantees), the integer element-wise work of each layer is compiled into fused kernels, and each decoding step is replayed as one CUDA graph. Table 17 compares it with BF16 and FP8 (W8A8, per-tensor scales) versions of the same model in SGLang [ZYX+24] on the same GPU. At batch 1, decoding is bound by reading the weights, and FO, with 8-bit weights, matches FP8 and is 30% faster than BF16. At batch 32, FO decodes at 79% of the FP8 rate: its exact attention and integer element-wise work cost more than FP8s, and its 8-bit matrix products run on an older-generation cuBLASLt kernel (a tile configuration of the Ampere generation) than SGLangs FP8 path. The largest gap is prefill, 2.7 times slower than FP8 at batch 32, because our engine prefills two sequences at time with exact integer attention while SGLang batches them through tuned kernels. These are costs of any exact scheme: proof about floating-point computation would first have to fix the order of every reduction, which current kernels do not do [HT25]. Where the time goes, and what would reduce it. Commitment, lookups and constraint terms account for almost all of the provers work. At long contexts, attention dominates, and the 16K proof already uses 72 of the GPUs 96 GiB. Every causal score entry costs one committed probability, one lookup and two constraint terms, and the probability must be committed because 49 it is lookup output. Sliding-window attention in most layers, as some current models use, would remove most of these entries. At short contexts, the prover is partly latency-bound; batching the many small sumchecks of layer into fewer, larger ones, and moving the remaining host-side claim arithmetic to the GPU, are the next steps there. Univariate skip for the first round [Gru24] would save an estimated 2% to 4%. Soundness parameters. The tightest terms of Table 2 are the queries (103.4 bits, of which 30 are proof of work) and the lookups (103.9 bits, of which 11 are proof of work). That margin is what composition with up to four recursive layers needs to stay above 100 bits overall. The lookup term depends on drawing one coefficient per tuple coordinate: with the powers of single challenge, which is common choice, tuples of arity seven would lose log 6 2.6 bits (Theorem 8.1) and the term would drop to 101.3 bits. Likewise, an exact left shift in 31-bit field needs bound on its input as well as on its output (Theorem 6.3). 2 Proof size and recursion. main proof of 106 to 477 MiB suits an auditor; returning one with every response is impractical. Reducing it has so far reduced the recursions input as well: the verifiers hashing fell by 4.2. The remaining verifier work is dominated by GKR challenges and leaf hashing; fewer GKR rounds (wider fraction trees, or fewer separate trees per domain) and larger work units would reduce both. Our BLAKE3 circuit is within 30% of the cell count assumed by the design, but the commitment of its trace is not yet measured, and an algebraic hash would make the recursion several times cheaper at the cost of further assumption. Zero knowledge. The main proof reveals evaluations of the trace and is meant for the requesting client. Multi-tenant proofs, closed weights that must stay secret, and publication of proofs all need zero knowledge; without it, about 1.9 104 proofs reveal the weights (Section 4), and batch reveals its prompts to every verifier of the batch. For multilinear arguments this requires hiding commitments (random symbols in every column, salted leaves), masked sumcheck and GKR messages in the style of [CFS17, XZZ+19], and lookup roots sent only per chunk. Each piece is standard; their combination with streamed, chunked prover needs its own analysis. Accuracy. FOs perplexity is 8.3% above BF16s, against 0.7% for FP8. Wider queries and keys would recover about third of the gap at an estimated 30 to 68% more proving time (Section 11.8); we have not located the rest. On Qwen3, better split of the existing score precision between queries and keys removed about quarter to half of the gap at no proving cost, which suggests that calibration still has room before formats must widen; finding integer formats that close the gap at small proving cost is the main open question for FO. Task benchmarks deserve the same scrutiny as perplexity: on Qwen3 few nats of logit error matter more on MMLU than on Qwen2.5 because the models own margins are smaller, and on GSM8K most of the loss of Qwen3-32B came from change of answer style. Generality. Besides Qwen2.5-32B, we evaluated two Qwen3 models: dense one with QK-norm and mixture of experts with 128 experts per layer (Section 5.6). Both reuse the protocol and add gadgets: QK-norm is the existing requantization and normalization applied per head row, and the experts are selected by threshold argument and dynamic multiset and multiplied by gathered sumchecks (Section 6.6). Other attention variants change the tile list. Other architectures change the gadget composition and keep the protocol.

sections.title: 13 Conclusion
sections.content: Sable shows that bit-exact proofs of production-size language model inference are feasible on one GPU. The full 64-layer Qwen2.5-32B is proven in 92.5 seconds for 4,096 tokens and in under seven minutes for 16,384 tokens, 41 to 50 times the time of the inference it attests and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. The same prover handles QK-norm and mixture of experts: it proves 4,096 tokens of Qwen3-32B in 121.8 seconds and of Qwen3-30B-A3B, whose tokens each use 8 of 128 experts per layer, in 84.7 seconds, and on both models FO stays within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. Three ingredients make this possible. An integer function fixes every rounding decision of the model. constraint system over 31-bit field never wraps, and its chunked lookups remain sound beyond lookups. streamed prover recomputes the witness where it would otherwise store it, and replays identical layers as GPU graphs. The same proof system proves BLAKE3 compressions at few microseconds each, which is the basis for compressing the main proof recursively. Served by an engine that computes it exactly, FO decodes as fast as FP8 at batch 1 and at 79% of its rate at batch 32. The remaining costs are proof that takes about 50 times the inference it attests, an integer function that loses accuracy against BF16, and, until the recursive layers with zero knowledge exist, proof suited to auditors of open-weight models. The next steps are those layers, verifier compiled as whole, and integer formats that recover the lost accuracy.
